n: In the seventh month — the season of Israel’s most sacred festivals — the returned exiles gathered in Jerusalem “as one man,” united in purpose.

f.g: Tishri (September–October), the month of the Feast of Trumpets, Day of Atonement, and Feast of Tabernacles.

n: Jeshua the priest and Zerubbabel the governor, with their fellow priests and kinsmen, rebuilt the altar first so sacrifices could resume as Moses’ law required. Worship came before walls or buildings.

f.w: as it is written in the law of Moses

n: They set the altar on its original foundation despite fear of surrounding peoples, and offered morning and evening sacrifices. They turned fear into faith by worshipping.
They kept the Feast of Tabernacles as written, offering the prescribed daily sacrifices — remembering God’s care during Israel’s wilderness journey, now fitting for exiles freshly returned.

f.g: In the prescribed number for each day.

n: After that they kept the regular offerings for new moons and all the Lord’s appointed festivals, plus freewill offerings. Israel’s calendar of worship came back to life.

f.g: The daily offering that was never to cease.

n: Sacrifices began on the first day of the seventh month, even though the temple foundation was not yet laid. They didn’t wait for perfect conditions to worship.
They paid stonecutters and carpenters, and traded food, drink, and oil with Sidon and Tyre for cedar logs floated to Joppa — just as Solomon had done for the first temple — with Cyrus’s permission.

f.w: the grant that they had of Cyrus

n: In the second month of their second year back (about 536 BC), Zerubbabel and Jeshua began the work, appointing Levites aged twenty and up to supervise. The second month echoes when Solomon began building.

f.w: from twenty years old and upward

n: Jeshua and his sons, Kadmiel and his sons, and the sons of Henadad worked together to oversee the workers. Unity of leaders made the work move.
When the foundation was laid, priests in their robes with trumpets and Levites with cymbals praised the Lord as David had ordained. They celebrated the beginning, not just the end.

They sang in alternating choirs: “He is good; his mercy endures forever toward Israel.” The people shouted with a great shout because the foundation was laid. The same song was sung at Solomon’s dedication.

f.w: he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever

n: But older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen Solomon’s temple wept aloud, while others shouted for joy. The elders grieved how humble the new start looked compared to the old glory.

f.w: that had seen the first house
f.g: Solomon’s temple had been destroyed about fifty years earlier.

n: No one could tell the shouts of joy from the sounds of weeping, and the noise was heard far away. Joy and grief mingled — a fitting picture of restoration after loss.

f.w: the noise was heard afar off
